Maine Online Casino Launch Could Miss Q1 2027 Target

Published October 21, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Maine's planned launch of regulated online casinos could slip past its first-quarter 2027 target if regulators end up making major changes to the state's proposed rules, the agency overseeing the rollout said this week.

A third round of rules, and a possible fourth

Maine Gambling Control Unit Executive Director Milt Champion told the agency's board on Tuesday that the state released its third published draft of iGaming rules on Sept. 30, with the public comment period on that draft running through Oct. 30. If regulators accept only minor tweaks from the comments received, the rulemaking process can move forward on its current track. But if they accept any major substantive changes, state law requires a fourth publication of the rules and another public comment period — effectively restarting part of the clock.

"We're in our third publication, and the comments are due the 30th of October," Champion said. "If we don't accept any more major substantive changes, we'll go on with the process. But if we do accept any major substantive changes, that will go through a fourth publication." He did not offer a revised target date, saying only that a fourth round "could" push the launch beyond Q1 2027.

Why the math works against a quick launch

Under Maine's rulemaking law, the Gambling Control Unit has up to 120 days after a comment period closes to formally adopt final rules, and the Office of the Attorney General then has up to 150 days from that same point to review and approve the rules for legality. Those are maximum windows rather than guarantees of delay, but stacked on top of a fourth comment period, they explain why regulators are flagging a real risk to the Q1 2027 target rather than treating it as locked in.

The backdrop: a tribal-exclusive market

Maine's online casino framework follows the same model as its existing sports betting market: a 2026 law (LD 1164), which Gov. Janet Mills allowed to become law without her signature despite a letter from the state's own gaming regulators asking her to veto it, gives Maine's four federally recognized Wabanaki tribes exclusive rights to operate online casinos. Three of the tribes already partner with Caesars for online sports betting, and the Passamaquoddy Tribe partners with DraftKings. The financial terms haven't changed through the rule revisions: an 18% tax on adjusted gross iGaming receipts, a $50,000 operator license fee, and a $500,000 bond requirement. If and when it launches, Maine would become the eighth U.S. state with a regulated online casino market. Separately, Champion noted the agency is hiring six new staff and has a new licensing portal online to help manage the workload, which he compared to the ramp-up ahead of the state's sports betting launch — "more so because it's a new product."

Why it matters

For players waiting on legal online casino access in Maine, the message is simple: expect the timeline to keep moving until a final rule package is actually adopted. The bigger pattern worth watching is one that's shown up in other states too — sequential rounds of rulemaking, each triggering its own comment period, are a common and underappreciated source of slippage between a state legalizing online casino gaming and it actually going live.
